newsitem.title: KENYA: Uganda sees record exports despite disease threat.
newsitem.headline: Uganda sees record exports despite disease threat.

text.p: Ugandan authorities on Tuesday posted record coffee exports in 1995/96 which they attributed to the outstanding success of economic liberalisation launched by the government of President Yoweri Museveni six years ago.

The authorities forecast an even better performance in the next year (October-September 1996/97) despite a disease threat but added that currency fluctuations meant that in dollar terms earnings for the crop would drop in 1995/96 from 1994/95.

A senior official at the Kampala-based state-owned Uganda Coffee Development Authority (UCDA) told Reuters that exports to the year ending 30 September 1996 touched 4.1 million 60-kg bags, the highest in Uganda's coffee exporting history. The exports compared with 2.8 million bags in 1994/95.
Coffee is Uganda's main commodity export and accounts for up to 70 percent of the country's total foreign exchange earnings.
"Production is going up due to conducive microeconomic policies that have ensured the farmers earn up to 80 percent of the international prices," the authority official said.
"We have recorded the highest amount of exports in history, at 4.1 million bags. In the next year, weather and other conditions permitting, we should see better," he added.

But the Switzerland-based Edm. Schluter & Co Ltd said early estimates put the crop at 3.3 million to 3.5 million bags. It added said the figure could be affected by recent hailstorm damage in September in the key growing central Buganda region.
Edm. Schluter & Co Ltd estimated in a report that Uganda's record exports would earn $380 million compared with $432 million the previous year.
It attributed the fall in earnings to curreny fluctuations.
The coffee official said the authority had appointed a task force to deal with the posibility of an outbreak of a disease named tracheomycosis, affecting the crop in neighbour Zaire.
"So far we have had no cases of the disease but we are on the lookout. We are determined that it does not spread to us at a time we are making headway in sales," the official added.
Edm. Schluter & Co said, "It is an encouraging reflection of the outstanding success of liberalisation of the industry."

"The liberalisation has been worked out over a period of dramatic market movements and it is clear that the main beneficiary has been the coffee farmer who now receives a very high percentage of the export price," the report said.
"In general though, the rains have been good," it said.
Museveni launched coffee reforms in 1990, announcing that four cooperative unions would be licensed to export coffee.
That was followed by other reforms, the latest being the offer for sale of a processing plant owned by the state Uganda Coffee Marketing Board, for which the single bid was poor.

"The increasing competitiveness of the internal market has made for a difficult season for some of the small exporters. The prices are adjusted constantly following moves on the international market," Edm. Schluter & Co Ltd said.

"Though the speed with which coffee is now moving through the system is greatly accelerated from two years ago, the margins at every level in the chain have tightened, as only the efficient operators are able to remain competitive," it added.
